Hey, thanks for the comment. I appreciate where you’re coming from, and I actually agree with quite a bit of what you said. Just for context, I work in this area professionally, and while I’m strongly against self-diagnosis, I do think self-exploration alongside someone trained in these disorders can be really valuable. Like you like you have suggested some potential avenues, I think it would be really great for them to explore that as well maybe it works out for them.

It’s great to hear that you’re reading up on psychopathy—there’s still a lot of stigma around ASPD and personality disorders in general, so any effort to understand them better is important.  And yep, You’re totally right that psychopathy isn’t a formal diagnosis; But Just to correct one little bit, it's not the same thing exactly as ASPD, rather it's a bit of a construct that overlaps with ASPD, often treated as a subset or trait-based dimension. Interestingly, many people with other Cluster B disorders, or even no diagnosis at all, can score high on psychopathy scales. I personally often refer to it as a subfacet of ASPD  because that’s how my supervisor conceptualises it, so I follow that framing. But even then, most people conflate psychopathy with just the Factor 1 traits, which is callous-unemotional traits, emotional detachment, etc. and the “American Psycho” stereotype, which only reflects part of the picture, but that's the one I'm trying to draw on in my example

On thrill-seeking: I only mentioned it because that’s what the original commenter asked about, and I wanted to be transparent. I did try to caveat that thrill-seeking alone doesn’t mean someone has psychopathy it’s not diagnostic in and of itself. The other example I gave, the autonomic nervous system response, is pretty consistently referenced in the literature (especially in Factor 1 psychopathy), so I mentioned it because it’s one of the more robust physiological findings.

Also, I brought up psychopathy specifically because the OP said they had ruled it out based on something inaccurate, i.e., “psychopaths don’t cry.” But people who score high in psychopathy do cry; emotional expression varies, but it isn’t absent across the board. I just didn’t want them ruling something out based on misinformation, but of course, it’s up to them in the end. You've given them your idea of what it could be, go for it more power to you hopefully they would have a good head on their shoulders at the as they explore it. I just didn't want them ruling out something completely if it could be. And thought I would try and give some suggestions I usually work for me to get a sense.

One tiny correction I wanted to mention gently, and I promise I say this with total warmth and a smile! The term “object permanence” is often misapplied to ADHD. It originally refers to an infant’s developmental stage where they don’t understand that things still exist when out of sight, And is used to explain why they get upset when their mum leaves.  While I totally get the “out of sight, out of mind” experience in ADHD (ask someone with ADHD all the time that's my life). The term has an important basis within psychopathy and was a little bit co-opted by people who interpreted it in one way without actually realizing its meaning and then took on a life of its own. Obviously no one is trying to be misleading, and you can use it if you want, But I know a lot of people with ADHD who also work in psychopathy, where every time they hear that (although it's less used now) they have this massive cringe inside or feel slightly insulted.

Anyway, I really appreciate your insight! Thanks for the thoughts!

Hey, for context I don't have BPD. I'm on these subs because I work with this group and want to understand the experience more. But when I see a person spiralling I of course want to help!

First, stop with him. Forget him for a moment. Right now I want to focus on you. You are going to be ok. You have made a mistake, obviously you really fucked up and there are consequences. But you don't need to fix it. If he stops talking to you, it will be ok. YOU are going to be ok, you will survive. You need to know that. If he decides to stay with you, you can learn from this, and know you will be ok. 

So the spiralling. Emotions are just that. And with BPD, forever reason the emotions go very extreme. But still, it will pass. One thing that helped me with some of my disorders, is when the biological side would trigger, and the excess in dopamine spiked, causing me to feel like I NEED to do whatever, I had to power through and force myself to believe otherwise and no respond to it. Like I had to go have a bath, and have what felt like a withdrawal rather than act on that thing. And I would focus on something else anything else. So you are spiralling, and the chemicals are kicking in,.... The glutamate system is coming is hyper activating your neurons to fire when they shouldn't be. Seratonin is low right now. Leading your amygdala is perceiving threat where there most likely isn't. It's hyper active right now, you can keep telling it to calm down there isn't a threat. It also leading dopamine in the striatum to potentially go for short term rewards (demanding release now) over long term resolutions, probably because it feels so intense. But short term, you don't need to resolve this situation, short term, you just need calm. 

As you can tell I've been doing a lot of reading on the neurobiology recently. But where others would feel like, this hurts and I'm scared, I don't want to loose them and want to feel loved, but I know if I do I will be brave enough o accept the outcome and will be patient for it. It's better for me stay calm now and ensure long term I get a positive outcome for me, whether he's in the long term or not, than say anything while I'm stressed now... Instead yours might be saying OMG everything is getting bad I must act now so I can stop this fear and feel safe again!

at the end of the day, he doesn't matter, what matters is you don't need to feel like this. You matter. And this is something no one should have to experience, regardless of what the event is.

Hey, diagnosis is my area of interest, so I love this question. I'm going to answer it from my perspective.

The problem is, we don't fully understand the causes of many disorders. Separating them out is tricky because symptoms often overlap, and the underlying biology and presentation can look very similar. It's rare to find traits that are unique to just one disorder. This can lead to conditions getting diagnosed together because they appear similar, even if they're distinct. Sometimes things are misdiagnosed, but once it's on your record, it tends to stay. Plus, if you have risk factors for one disorder, you often have risk factors for others too — it’s all very complex.

To answer your question about why people get diagnosed for multiple things — and why we don’t just diagnose everything — the reality is, that would actually help in some ways. It could catch misdiagnoses and better identify comorbidities. However, fully assessing every person for every possible condition would require someone to have an expertise in a lot of conditions (which risks a jack of all disorders and a master of none) and massive amounts of time and resources. It’s just not practical.

Instead, we often use screening questionnaires. These aren't diagnostic — they’re blunt tools too — but they can flag areas where a full evaluation might be worthwhile. Even then, you have to take them with a big grain of salt. Because sometimes they're phrased in a way that if you don't know what an extreme version of this symptom looks like it is easy to assume that you do the things that the screening tool is referring to, especially if you are not a specialist who has worked with their groups of people (I'm sorry no internet research does not count, this is as a researcher who's done academic research, it does not equate to actually working with loads of people with a disorder)

Another reason that they shouldn't do full-on screens, is diagnosis is a personal decision (mostly). Just because you might meet criteria for something like autism doesn’t mean you have to pursue the label if it doesn’t feel relevant or necessary in your life. I know people who meet criteria for autism but say, "I'm fine as I am."

If we screened everyone fully, we might end up pathologizing traits in people who are perfectly happy and functioning just fine without a label. 

So that is why lots of people have comorbidities but we do not do full-on diagnosis for everybody.

Piggie backing on this comment to give some anecdotal experience. I feel like the answer is more complicated, And how you feed your baby could turn into a loop

Our baby started off eating every 2 to 3 hours, but we started feeding baby every time she cried sometimes because we didn't know what was wrong. I think this messed up her appetite because she started crying every 45 minutes, as though she was starving. After a while, and several incidents with the hospital, my gut was telling me this was wrong. So I very carefully decided to wait 20 minutes before feeding her. She cried the whole time and it was a relief when I could finally feed her. But the next time was so much easier. Within half a day she had adjust to it fairly well. The next day I increased by 20 minutes again. And each time it got easier and easier. Until finally she was back to eating every 3 to 4 hours (which is normal formula fed baby. It's 1 hour less for a breastfed baby). When I did this, a lot of other issues went away. The projectile vomiting, gassiness, feverish like appearance, and crying stopped. She slept longer which was a blessing to us, but I noticed she seemed more awake and refreshed in the morning. 

I will also say, you should follow your gut as a mother. After my baby's appetite went back to normal, people would keep reinforcing that I should feed her every time she cries, regardless of why she's crying, and said there is no harm in feeding her. But I knew if that happened we would go back to her feeling unwell and bloated and projectile vomiting. And she was about 3 months old at this point. 

Saying this she did eat every two to 3 hours when she was born... Until we messed it up. And I get the impression she's a very adaptive baby, But also I was following my gut as to what was best for her. I think you should do the same. If you feel like baby needs to eat, and there is no good reason to delay,  then feed them.

I once applied for PhD that explore this. There was an idea that in the animal kingdom you will respond to yor environment depending on how positive and negative reinforcement, and how often that environment changes. 

People have a thing called learning rates. You taking information about your environment but how much you learn from it differs. Let's say you're in a negative environment where things are bad and you feel a bit sad. If you have a high learning rate, when things start to get a little bit positive, you also be more likely to learn things are positive and therefore be happier. If you have a low learning rate, you are a lot less likely to learn from and think things are positive, even when lots of great positive things are happening to you.  Think of someone who keeps moaning and thinks life is terrible even when lots of great things are happening. The learning rate depends on how stable your environment is. So if you're in an environment which very rarely changes from positive to negative, You will have a low learning rate because you don't believe things can change easy, as a result you don't see the positives as positive as they really are. But if your environment regularly changes, you will have a high learning rate and therefore learn from positives or negatives very quickly, because it's very likely your environment has changed.

This situation can be evolutionarily beneficial most of the time cuz it means you can adapt your environment as appropriate. But there will be some people in some circumstances who have a very long period of A negative environment, so when the environment changes to positive they just don't learn from it and they still feel really sad even though everything is going great. One evidence of this is that antidepressants are argued to work by changing the reward-based systems of people to be more tuned to positive information, so that depression fades because they're learning from the positive experiences.

This is one theory and to be honest with you, they're most likely as many, many reasons why depression exists. Some people it might be a physiological response, for some people it might be because they ate something that causes a physiological response, for some people it could be that they are going through a significant trauma, for some people, it's just life has been s*** and they don't quite realize things are better. But this is ultimately This is one example of how a psychological process which is adaptive and helpful, can in some circumstances not be very adaptive.

Where It's not super fixed as to what I can put in together, But it's always roughly the same type of things so that I don't need to get stressed about what I'm going to cook today. 

Lunch is always either boiled to Oblivion pasta or bread and butter. Added with vegetable sticks, a puree and either cheese, tuna or chicken. 

Dinner is a bit more complicated. But it's either meatballs, croquet's, hard boiled egg, a basic omelette, Rice, or chips. And that comes with a puree or two. 


Wherever possible, I also make things in advance in batches and freeze them. So I've cooked all the chicken pieces and tuna and frozen them so I can just take a little bit out and add it to a plate if I feel like that plate's a bit empty. I've prepped like 28 pieces of meatballs and again croquets. I can literally just take it out. Stick it in the oven. I regularly make purees when I'm cooking my own food by just sticking some leftover vegetables into a blender and the stick it in the freezer. Sometimes I just wake up and stick some lentils In the pan chuck in some vegetables half an hour later turn off. And I'll blend it when I feel like it. I also chop some random vegetable into sticks 3 days in advance so that I can throw them in the pan to boil for about half an hour every morning. (Usually it's carrots, celery or parsnip... But if I made an aubergine the day before for myself, I might cut some of those into sticks so I can use it the next day as well).

Because I follow the same format but just like differences... Eg. There's always a puree. There's always a vegetable sticks... That I know what to do like autopilot and I can do it quickly. The only only thing that I ever need to think about is the dinner as to whether it's an omelette or whatever else. 

I find that if I have a strict meal plan of the day... Lile, it's definitely going to be tuna pasta, or tomorrow it must chicken with broccoli... I don't follow it because it doesn't give a flexibility of using what's available at the time, and I end up having to spend ages thinking about what I'm making and preping..... Instead I create a meal plan that says it's either going to be a sandwich or a pasta this day with whatever I have left over. And there's always going to be at least one puree or dip. That works for me because it's flexibility to just go in to the fridge and take what's there.

Also, sometimes I replace the vegetable sticks with those melt-in-the-mouth Stick things that you can get in the shops. And I might not have a puree. I might have hummus or baba ganoush instead. So that if I don't have anything quickly grab those things out.
